blocks.text: Three questions with the same name and a growing difficulty. They share one lesson because each one builds on the last:

items: **Path Sum (I)** — given `root` and `targetSum`, is there a **root-to-leaf** path whose values add up to `targetSum`? Return `true` or `false`.
**Path Sum II** — return **every** root-to-leaf path that adds up to `targetSum`, as lists of values.
**Path Sum III** — **count** the paths that add up to `targetSum`, where a path may **start and end anywhere**, as long as it goes **downward** (parent to child).

blocks.alt: The tree 5, 4, 8, 11, null, 13, 4, 7, 2, null, null, 5, 1 with target 22. Two root-to-leaf paths add up to 22: 5, 4, 11, 2 and 5, 8, 4, 5. So Path Sum I answers true and Path Sum II returns both paths.

blocks.code:
root = [5, 4, 8, 11, null, 13, 4, 7, 2, null, null, 5, 1],  targetSum = 22
Path Sum I   -> true
Path Sum II  -> [[5, 4, 11, 2], [5, 8, 4, 5]]

root = [10, 5, -3, 3, 2, null, 11, 3, -2, null, 1],  targetSum = 8
Path Sum III -> 3      (5 -> 3,  5 -> 2 -> 1,  -3 -> 11)

blocks.text: The key idea for I and II: instead of adding values up and comparing at the end, carry the **remaining** amount down. Each node subtracts its value; a leaf that receives exactly **0** remaining finishes a matching path. (Values can be negative, so you can't stop early just because the sum got big.)
Path Sum I — 1. Brute force: list every root-to-leaf sum
**Time O(n), space O(n)** — it stores a sum per leaf and always walks the whole tree, even if the very first path matches.
Path Sum I — 2. Best solution: carry what's remaining, stop at the first match

**Time O(n), space O(h)**, and `||` stops as soon as one side finds a path. Note the leaf check: an empty tree is **not** a path, so `hasPathSum(null, 0)` must be false — that's why the check happens at leaves, not at null.
Path Sum II: collect the paths with backtracking

Now we need the paths themselves. Use the backtracking pattern from **Binary Tree Paths**: keep one shared path, push on the way down, pop on the way back up, and **copy** it into the answer at a leaf with 0 remaining. (Copy, not the list itself — it keeps changing.)

blocks.caption: The caption under each node is the amount still needed after it.

blocks.code:
def path_sum(root, target):
    result = []
    path = []
    def dfs(node, remaining):
        if node is None:
            return
        path.append(node.val)
        remaining -= node.val
        if node.left is None and node.right is None and remaining == 0:
            result.append(path[:])          # a leaf that uses up the target exactly
        dfs(node.left, remaining)
        dfs(node.right, remaining)
        path.pop()                          # backtrack
    dfs(root, target)
    return result

blocks.text: **Time O(n · h)** in the worst case — copying a path of length up to h for each matching leaf — **space O(h)** besides the output.
Path Sum III — 1. Brute force: start a search at every node
Paths can now start anywhere. So for **every** node, count the downward paths **starting there** that add up to the target — a Path-Sum-style walk without the leaf rule (any node can end a path).

blocks.alt: Path Sum III on 10, 5, -3, 3, 2, null, 11, 3, -2, null, 1 with target 8. Three downward paths add up to 8: 5 → 3, 5 → 2 → 1, and -3 → 11. None of them starts at the root or ends at a leaf necessarily.

blocks.text: **Time O(n · h)** — every node re-walks its whole subtree, so a chain costs O(n²) — **space O(h)**.
Path Sum III — 2. Best solution: prefix sums on the current path

Borrow the trick from **Subarray Sum Equals K**. Let `sum` be the total from the root down to the current node. A downward path from some ancestor's child down to here adds up to `sum − (prefix at that ancestor)`. So the number of good paths **ending here** is the number of earlier prefixes on the current path equal to **`sum − target`**. Keep those prefixes in a hash map — and remove each one when you leave its node, so only the current path's prefixes are counted.

blocks.alt: Prefix sums on one path: 10, 15 (after 5), 18 (after 3). At node 3 the sum is 18; 18 − 8 = 10 is an earlier prefix (the root's), so one path ending at 3 adds up to 8: it starts just below 10, at 5 → 3.

blocks.caption: The list shows the prefix sums on the current path; they come off as the walk backs up.

blocks.code:
from collections import defaultdict

def count_path_sums(root, target):
    seen = defaultdict(int)                 # prefix sum -> times seen on the current path
    seen[0] = 1
    count = 0
    def dfs(node, total):
        nonlocal count
        if node is None:
            return
        total += node.val                   # root-to-here sum
        count += seen[total - target]       # paths ending here that add up to target
        seen[total] += 1
        dfs(node.left, total)
        dfs(node.right, total)
        seen[total] -= 1                    # leaving: this prefix is off the path
    dfs(root, 0)
    return count

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h)** for the recursion plus the map (at most one entry per node on the current path, though stale zero-count keys may linger). On LeetCode this function is also called `pathSum`; it is renamed here so the three parts can sit side by side. Values up to 10⁹ make the running sums overflow 32-bit integers — hence `long`.

blocks.alt: Path Sum I with early stopping: O(n) time, O(h) space. Path Sum II with backtracking: O(n times h) time, O(h) space. Path Sum III brute force: O(n times h) time, O(h) space. Path Sum III with prefix sums: O(n) time, O(h) space.

items: **Empty tree** — I: false (even for target 0); II: `[]`; III: 0.
**A node with one child isn't a leaf** — `[1, 2]`, target 1: I is false, because 1 alone isn't a root-to-leaf path.
**Negative values** — `[-2, null, -3]`, target -5: true. Never prune because a partial sum got "too big".
**Zeros (III)** — `[0, 1, 1]`, target 1: paths 0→1 (twice) and 1 (twice): 4. Prefix counts, not a set, handle repeated prefixes.
**Path Sum IV** — the tree is given as three-digit codes (depth, position, value); rebuild positions and run Path Sum.
**Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum** — any path, even one that bends through a node; return the largest sum.
**Subarray Sum Equals K** — Path Sum III on an array: the same prefix-sum counting.
**Sum Root to Leaf Numbers** — combine the values along each path into a number instead.
